newsitem.title: CHINA: China says to send hijacker back to Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: China says to send hijacker back to Taiwan.

text.p: China on Thursday gave in to Taiwan's demands to repatriate a man suspected of forcing a Taiwanese airliner to the mainland this month, but called on the island to send back 16 Chinese hijackers in return.
"Liu Shan-chung... will be repatriated to Taiwan after necessary investigations are made," the Xinhua news agency said, quoting the semi-official Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Straits.
It did not give a date for the repatriation of Liu, who is suspected of hijacking a domestic Taiwanese airliner on March 10 and forcing it to China's southeastern city of Xiamen.

The association handles bilateral ties in the absence of formal links between Beijing and Taipei, rivals since the communists won the Chinese civil war and drove the defeated Nationalists into exile on Taiwan in 1949.
Taiwan welcomed the offer but said it needed formal notice from Beijing before the matter could be handled further.

"This will be positive for our future talks on hijacker repatriation," said Jonathan Liu, director of the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council, in reference to semi-official talks with Beijing stalled since mid-1995.
Taiwan had demanded Liu's repatriation while Chinese officials debated whether to send him back or prosecute him.
China said it was repatriating Liu in line with a pact reached in 1990 but which was never signed.
Liu, 45, a jobless journalist, doused himself with gasoline and commandeered the airliner to China, complaining of political repression at home.
China returned the plane, other passengers and crew on the same day, but kept Liu in custody.
The Far East Air Transport jet, carrying 150 passengers and eight crew, was on a scheduled flight from Taiwan's southern city of Kaohsiung to Taipei when it was forced to China.
Beijing called for reciprocity after agreeing to release Liu.
"We hope that the Taiwan side will take prompt measures to repatriate hijackers, in a bid to join hands in cracking down on hijacking," the association official said.
Liu of Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council declined to make any commitment on Beijing's demand that Taipei return all 16 hijackers, most of whom are in jail on the island.
Taipei has offered to return two of the Chinese who hijacked planes to the island between April 1993 and June 1994.
Air piracy fell off sharply after Beijing launched a major drive to improve normally lax security at its airports.

The last hijacking of a Taiwanese airliner to China was in May 1986, when the pilot of a Boeing 747 cargo plane owned by Taiwan's flag carrier China Airlines commandeered the jet and flew it to Guangzhou.
The defecting pilot was hailed as a hero and made a civil aviation official. Beijing returned the jet and two crew members who did not want to stay in China after talks in Hong Kong.
